author: buchanan_robert
text:
But, when the little dog barked at them, they fled,
Not one of them would stop for a few moments,
To hear what news they brought or give some news back,
The king himself could not make them stay a while,
Nor even try his best to turn their minds from flight;

author: cushag
text:
“The little maiden went down to the mill pond,

With her father, who lived near where they did live.”

They went down and looked at the ducks in the water—

They were swimming like stars above the billow;

Her father said “There are stars floating on the water!”

And pointing to them in the sunlit sky,

He told her that all night long when the moon is shining,

The fish swim past her eyes as she sleeps by.”

And then one day, the girl came out to the river,

Not looking for anything, or expecting

At night when all are still asleep,
When day has slept beneath the sea
In silence deep,
How still is everything around!
The world at rest—the air is soundless,
All shadows deep—no noise or stir,
No life at all,
Nothing stirs, not even the heart
Of one who sleeps in darkness here.

Then I can hear again—how clear!
My dear ones call me home from fear.
The children say, ‘Good-night!’ to each other.
I cannot hear them any more.

My little girl has

author: buchanan_robert
text:
When I first came into this world, my brother said—
“There is a little baby!” but they all were gay.
One thing only did he say, “It will not live.”
Oh! those that knew me thought so too, for I had pale eyes.

In time when children gathered at their play
The doctor told them who I was, “This is the boy who died,”
Said they—“He looks just as you tell us,
But oh! how can we believe it? It cannot be true.”
 

And now I am grown up,

author: buchanan_robert
text: There is no doubt that one of the best books which has come from our new literature is Mrs Oliphant's The Life and Death of Richard Yea and Dick Yi—a book whose merits have been much extolled, but seldom sufficiently appreciated. It is impossible for any woman who knows how great are the obstacles against which this fine work has had to contend to fail to admire the heroic courage and tenacity of spirit displayed by those who have wrought so beautifully in this direction.

author: cushag
text:
When I got to the church, I set down beside you.
I said, " Now, Mary, what do ye want?"
"Oh!" says she, " I want a husband."
And then, Mary goes on to say,
That since her father left home, and went away,
She has never had no husband;
So now I am going to get one myself.

author: emily_dickinson
text:
When you see a man go with a woman
Who hasn’t got a dress on,

Be sure that he's not as good a man
As most men in the town;

For if he does, she will come to meet him

Me, that used to be a gentleman—
An' my husband too,

Was once as good as any lord in England,

But we were out o' work an' poor.

When Johnny found out our condition,

He set about makin' money ;

So he took up with his gun an' powder,

While me had to do the laundry.

author: cushag
text:
" What you doin', Mary ? " says the man;

Says he : " Go cut that firewood !"

Mary answers him back— " Oh no ; you must help to cut it."

He cuts a few sticks, and then goes home.

Then Mary takes out her knitting-needle and sews away, while the man sits there smoking his pipe.

author: cushag
text:
I see you in the mornin', with yer hand on yer head,

Mournin' over your troubles ; it looks so sad.

Your wife's not dead, nor your children starved to death,

Nor have ye no money-lender after yer hearth.

Perhaps ye may be thinkin' that I'll give ye some advice;

But if I tell ye anythin' about 'ealth or wealth,

Yer mind will go off somethin' else, which I don't know much about,

For I never got out o' bed but

author: emily_dickinson
text:
I heard a bird sing on the wing
 A sweet wild song as it flew;
 There was no joy so dear to me
 As that sweet bird's song when he sang true.

author: john_keats

text:

That ran away from home;
He left his bit and bridle,
And wouldn't come back no more.

author: emily_dickinson
text:
I love the sunshine, - O! how sweet it is;
 The meadow flowers that nod so gracefully,
 The honeybee, - and all his busy life,
 That fills the air with songs from morn till night.
 How I delight to watch him on the wing,
 As he alights upon a flowery tree,
 His graceful form as he makes merry song,
 Whence comes this sweetness in the atmosphere?

author: emily_dickinson
text:
One day when I was sitting at work,
 A bird came fluttering near,
 With folded wings she sat upon the floor
 And cried for bread or beer.
 "You don't know me," said I, but I knew her,
 For her mother was my friend,
 She lived not far away, and had a house,
 But no bread or no beer

author: john_keats
text:
At last he reached the chapel’s door;
Wherein was painted on the wall-paper,
The story of our Saviour, from His birth
To death and resurrection; which work
Was done in Flanders by great Rubens there:
In this, as well as other holy things,
His pious fancy found delight; and here
He spent three hours, till time for supper drew near

author: john_masefield
text:
The little boy, not seeing her approach,
Had dropped behind, when suddenly she stopped,
As if uncertain where or what to find,
For such was her condition and mind;
Then stooping down, to take him in her arms,
She gently lifted up her infant charms,
While from their tender hands the waxen fingers
Drew out those flowers which grew upon their fingers,
Which then again they put between their bosoms,
With all their sweetness and perfume thus posies.

Then at the end of this short space of time
(For I had heard no sound but footsteps clink)
There came to me an opening in the gloom:
Through it one foot went first, then followed on
The other, making its way so slowly down;
But as the head grew clearer, I begun
To see what were the shapes that moved around;
They were, indeed, those very persons we mourn—
My friends, my children, my parents all!

author: john_keats
text: The moon was shining in her might, And all the birds were silent, For she had stopped their wings, And tied their feet with golden strings. The hills and valleys were bright As if they'd been set in jewels; And on the river-side stood The queenliest flowers that growed By night, When it is dark, 'Tis better for the moon than day.

author: john_keats
text:
This was the dwelling of old Priam’s son;
But all the courtly pomp is vanished long.

author: john_masefield
text:
"The house had been built for two brothers
By a father who loved them both as one;
So they grew up together in their room,
Till each went forth into his separate doom,
One working at the pit-head, and another,
At the machine shop, where he turned out clever things."

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
"What is man that he should be mindful
Of his Creator? And what is woman
But a beast in whom this mind can dwell?
The earth is full of both sexes. All must die.
Let them but know each other and forget
Their difference, while they live, for death is one."

"In a cottage in the middle of the country,
There lived an old man and his daughter,
With one eye that never shut until he died,
The other one blinked for years and then expired."

author: john_masefield
text:
"But when I had my children in the house,
They never seemed like mine at all to me;

As soon as they were born, it was too late--
How could a woman know what she had meant?"

author: john_masefield
text: "There are not many people who do not know that I have a very poor memory as regards names and dates. This is quite true. It has always been so. I cannot recall what happened ten years ago, or any date in history which does not come within twenty-five years. But my recollection of scenes is wonderful. If ever I see a place again, I remember it as well as if I had seen it only yesterday. That was what enabled me to describe the castle at Tintagel so vividly."

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text: On Sunday night the weather was fine, and we started off from the jetty with our wind in spite of our light airs; it came up very strong during the first half-hour or so, and gave us plenty of canvas to keep her going; she made about five miles an hour, when suddenly the breeze went dead flat. We were close to shore at the time and had not more than two hours sail before we should have been forced to put back; however, as all the water is salt round here, the skipper told me he thought he would have no difficulty in getting enough fresh, so

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text:
My son, my darling boy, will you take care
of mother, now that father has gone away,

To seek his fortune in foreign lands, where
men are all alike, wherever they may be?

I shall need her help, when she is well enough;
she was always good and kind to us both.

We have come here to live together while we
can; so do not let her go, or leave her alone.

I see my way clear now to get up, and go to the
sea again; so in due course I may be laid on it, too.

author: robert_frost
text: He who doth me wrong doth himself more harm than I;

I remember well when I had just turned twelve;

My father's house, in which we dwelt for awhile,

Was full of children, all but one or two, who fled—

To what end? Who knows? But they did not die.

text: The sea-breeze from morning to night, in hot summer weather, blows upon this place like a whirlwind. Its temperature is high as that of Damascus; so are its nights also, on account of the excessive heat during the day. It has no rains at all, nor any rivers, but there are many springs of water, and some ponds where fish may be taken, which have been made for the people. author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
robert_frost
text:
"You know your way," said I, "along the road?"
"No." 'Well then, you'll never get along without
a guide." And I got one. A boy had come in
From work; he knew my way well enough. We walked
Together. He said nothing—as if he didn't
know me. His face was not unkindly turned,
But just blank. At last we reached the house.
The door opened. The child who lived here stood
Within, smiling kindly at the strangers.

author: stephen_crane
text:

Against me, just for this one thoughtlessness.
If you see people doing mean things every day,
And if they seem not to care very much
About anything, you mustn't suppose
They are less human than yourself, but think

"Why do you let me go out?

My father died long ago,
With all his money spent,

Now you must know,

author: robert_frost
text:
"The poetical spirit
Is not so strong as once it seemed;—we see
That something more than nature has gone out
Of our poor world. It may not seem strange
To you, but here we feel a sort of pain
At all this empty poetry.—It seems
As if these times were too prosaic for verse.
Our souls are not their own, we want some one
Whom we may call our master. Not even Wordsworth
Will do now. He must be a man who wrote
His life in verse and lived it also."

author: robert_frost
text:
"The young man came in one day last week,
With eyes of hungry curiosity;
But, when he went away again that night,
His face had all its old vacant look."

author: stephen_crane
text:
The lark is the bird of joy; 
 The sun shall give him his day.
 He sings when the world's awake,
 And sleeps with its close-shut eye.

author: stothert_james_a
text:
Two old women sat on a wall;
One was bald, and one had hair.
The bald woman said, “My friend,
Will you let me have a comb?”
“I will not,” said she with the hair.

The King's daughter came home late one night; She could not find her way. She saw some lights at an open door, So she went into it. When she had gone inside, The maid who opened the door Put up her fingers and called for help. It was too dark for the king's daughters to see. One of them was blind from birth. Another had lost both her eyes in war. The third wore no clothes. What are you going to do if your friend is sad?

author: stephen_crane
text:
The old woman and her cat
 Ate bread for breakfast.
 The old woman ate all hers first;
 She let the cat eat some.
 It was a lovely summer day!

author: stephen_crane
text: There was once a woman who had no children. She sat all day long watching her clock; and every night she went into church and prayed for a son to come home from his studies at Cambridge. And so it came about that she had a son, and he returned one evening with great pleasure to his mother's arms. But when they met she clasped him to her bosom and cried, "I have lost my darling!"

author: stothert_james_a
text: To-morrow we shall wake and know each other —

author: thomas_hardy
text:
For Nature's breath from heaven was breathed upon thee,
Thou art her offspring; yet a part she holds :
From God’s great mind thou art derived and known;
The soul thou art, for souls were made before man’s fleshly body mould.

author: stothert_james_a
text:
I see a Spirit near me now,

A voice I hear and know not how :—
The air, so still before, is rife

With whispers from another life.

I cannot speak; but if he would say
To me that he was with me then,
How gladly would my heart receive the gladness!
Ah! were there something that we had seen
Together ere this world came down? —
A token yet perhaps remain,
That once some friend had come his way,
Who sought him there beyond the bound ?
A sign that shows the hand divine

author: stothert_james_a
text:
I have a world within my soul.
It needs no light from any star;
There’s not one dim spot where a shade can roll,
For Love and Truth are there, my dear!
The heart must be strong which knows not fear;
But I know you — so now I need
No aid from anything but you, for me
To make this bright life that shall never end.

author: thomas_hardy
text:
I Knew a lady whose eyes were blue.
 I never saw anyone who could smile quite like that.

author: william_wordsworth
text:
The heart can ne’er be tired
 Of hearing tell how sweet was
 The scene where erst it knelt;
 Nor need its love forget
 That spot amid all lands
 Where first its footsteps led!

The heart is full of love for thee;
 The eyes are wet with tears; but ah!
 What can they tell? But only say,
 How beautiful thou art compared
 To all that now I leave behind.
 Thy face is lovely in its smile;
 Its beauty’s worth my soul to give.
 Yet it is not alone thy face
 That I shall miss. In thought I feel
 That every trait of thine hath gone
 With thee,—the very air that breathes
 Around thy form, its fragrance stealing
 Into mine senses. Now farewell,
 My dearest one

author: thomas_hardy
text: We looked about us, saying that this is the one place! The wind-swept heath, those hills with white clouds overhead, the quiet river running along its level course among them, were all ours, though but for an hour or two. And if they are not ours now, how much more may we be sure of having them some day? When the time comes for us to go home, then surely we shall find what it was like before us. Let others go, or stay, as pleases them; let them take pictures, leave inscriptions on trees

author: thomas_hardy
text:
There are some flowers that never fade,
    And yet they ever change,
The face of heaven is always fair,
Yet it is always changing.

If you had but one day to live,
You need not ask me how to use,
How spend your precious little time;
I know I'd spend my last day just like the first.—R.W.S.

author: william_wordsworth
text:
I come from England. O ye blessed Isles!
 Whose hills and groves have nursed me up in peace!
 Where shall I find your likeness? Where can I trace
 The loveliness of your features in these faces?

author: buchanan_robert
text: The sun has gone down, the night is come, The stars are in their courses set, And all things seem to tell me so, But what shall I believe or doubt? That which I am most sure of is, That at this very moment when the shadows fall across the fields, And when those silvery curtains, like wings of angels spread above us, And the stillness steals over everything, And even the birds have ceased to sing and call—at such an hour I cannot help feeling that there is something near me; Something nearer than man or woman, Or child or brute can ever be:

I never saw the lovely scene
 Of Salisbury Plain from up so high.
 My heart was struck at first sight--and when
 The evening star did slowly rise,
 The crimson light shone o’er the plain,
 And round the white chalk hill, where stood
 Our soldiers in their bright array.
 
The sun set in his golden chariot;
 His beams were like diamonds far away,
 To mark the battle-field of Heaven,
 Where angels fought beneath the ray.
 Oh! what a solemn picture it presents!
 A hundred thousand souls are lost!

author: william_wordsworth
text:

O dearest friend! 'tis hard, indeed, hard, very, To lose thee! I know what will come over me When thou art gone--a sense of awful vacancy, A void of happiness so wide and dreary That it would fill up all the world before I knew How

text:

 Against those that rise against me." Then came
 The chorus of all armies:—"The battle rages!"
 No more then could I doubt but that we ought
 To fight. So now I see what was before

 Told me once (and he knows more than I) that God
